title: The Retention Trap: Why Churn Analysis Alone Won't Save Your Product
excerpt: Most teams treat retention like a math problem — measure churn, segment the lost users, and try to win them back. But retention isn't an analytics problem. It's a product thesis problem, and chasing churn numbers without understanding why people leave is how you end up optimizing the wrong thing.
content:
Here's a scenario that plays out at startups everywhere: your monthly churn ticks up from 4% to 6%, and suddenly retention is all anyone talks about. You dig into the data. You segment by cohort, by plan tier, by acquisition channel. You find that users who don't hit the "aha moment" in their first week are three times more likely to leave. So you ship an onboarding tooltip, a welcome email sequence, and a redesigned getting-started page.

Two months later, churn is still 6%. What went wrong?

You solved the signal, not the problem. And that's the retention trap: confusing what churn data tells you with what churn data means.

What Churn Data Actually Tells You

Churn is a lagging indicator. By the time someone cancels, they've been disengaged for weeks or months — they just finally made it official. Looking at churn numbers is like studying skid marks instead of learning to drive. You can describe the accident in perfect detail without understanding what caused it.

This matters because churn analysis is fundamentally descriptive. It tells you who left, when, and sometimes what they did before leaving. It does not tell you why they left, whether they're coming back, or what would have kept them. Those are causal questions, and descriptive data can't answer them.

The Three Fallacies of Churn-Driven Retention

1. The "Win Back" Fallacy

If you know which users churned, you can re-engage them with a discount, a feature announcement, or a "we miss you" email. This works — sometimes. But it treats retention as a marketing problem when it's usually a product problem. Users who leave because the product doesn't solve their problem will come back for a month on a discount and leave again when the discount expires. You haven't retained them; you've rented them.

2. The "Feature Gap" Fallacy

Churn analysis often reveals patterns like "users who don't use feature X are twice as likely to churn." The natural conclusion: build more of feature X. But correlation isn't mechanism. Users might not use feature X because they're power users who've already solved their problem another way, or because feature X is poorly designed and everyone avoids it, or because the users who would benefit from it never made it past onboarding. The pattern is real. Your explanation of it might be wrong.

3. The "Fix the Leak" Fallacy

Retention is often framed as a bucket with a hole: stop the leaks and the water level rises. This metaphor is almost always wrong. Most products don't have a few identifiable "leaks" — they have dozens of small friction points that collectively erode retention. Plugging one doesn't move the needle because users find another way to slip away. And some "leaks" aren't leaks at all — they're users who got what they needed and left, which is a success, not a failure.

What To Do Instead

Start with the product thesis, not the churn number. Ask: what is the core value this product promises, and how would someone know they've received it? That answer — the moment of value delivery — is your real retention mechanic. Everything else is optimization around the edges.

Then measure whether people reach that moment. Not whether they stay — whether they get it. A user who reaches the value moment and leaves is a different problem than a user who never reaches it. The first might be unavoidable (they got what they needed) or fixable (they didn't realize what they had). The second is always a product problem.

Segment by outcome, not by demographic. "Users who experienced X" is more useful than "users on the Pro plan" because it tells you something about causality rather than just correlation. If you can't segment by something causal — did they use the core feature, did they reach their goal, did they experience the value — then your retention analysis is just describing the shape of the problem, not illuminating it.

The One Question That Matters

Instead of "why are people leaving?" ask "what did the people who stayed actually do?" Retention is not the absence of churn. It's the presence of something — a habit, a result, a workflow, a payoff. Find what that something is, make sure new users can reach it, and measure how many do. The churn number will take care of itself — or at least, it'll mean something when it moves.

title: Customer Discovery: The Questions That Actually Matter
excerpt: Most customer interviews go wrong before the first question is asked. Teams show up with a script full of leading questions and leave with confirmation bias disguised as insight. The difference between a useless interview and a breakthrough one isn't the number of questions — it's the quality of what you choose not to ask.
content:
The Interview Nobody Needed

A PM schedules thirty minutes with a potential user. They open a doc with fourteen questions, all carefully worded to be "open-ended." They ask about pain points, current workflows, and what the user would want in a solution. The user answers thoughtfully. The PM leaves feeling like they learned something. Two weeks later, they build the feature the user described. It flops.

What happened? The user gave accurate answers to the wrong questions. They described their current behavior honestly, expressed mild interest in the proposed solution, and the PM mistook expressed interest for validated need. This is the most common failure mode in customer discovery, and it's entirely avoidable.

The Questions to Stop Asking

These questions feel productive but reliably produce garbage:

  • "Would you use a product that did X?" — People are polite. They will tell you yes to almost anything that sounds like it might help. This measures social agreeableness, not intent.
  • "How much would you pay for X?" — Pricing discovered through direct questioning is fiction. People have no reference point for a product that doesn't exist yet. Their guesses reflect their desire to be helpful, not their actual willingness to pay.
  • "What's your biggest pain point?" — Everyone has dozens. The question is too broad to surface the specific problem worth solving, and the answer is usually whatever pain is most top-of-mind today, not what they'd prioritize solving.
  • "What features would you want?" — This is how you end up building feature factories. Users are great at describing their problems in their own language and terrible at designing solutions. Ask about the problem, not the feature.

The Questions That Actually Work

The goal of a discovery interview is not to gather opinions — it's to observe behavior. Opinions are cheap and often wrong. Behavior is expensive and usually right. Every question should either surface a specific behavior or reveal the context around one.

"Tell me about the last time you encountered this problem." — Not "do you have this problem" but "when was the last time, and what did you do about it?" The last-time framing forces specificity. People can lie about their habits; they struggle to lie about a specific recent event without tripping over details.

"What did you try before coming to this conclusion?" — Every problem has a history. The solutions someone has already attempted tell you more about the problem's urgency and their sophistication than anything they'll say about a hypothetical future product. If they haven't tried anything, the problem might not be painful enough to solve.

"What would happen if you didn't solve this?" — This reveals stakes. A problem worth solving has consequences for not solving it. If the answer is "nothing much," you might be solving a nice-to-have dressed up as a must-have. If the answer is "I'd lose my job" or "the business would lose $50K a month," you're onto something.

"Walk me through how you do this today, step by step." — Shadowing in verbal form. People describe their workflow inaccurately when asked directly; watch what they actually do, or have them narrate a real instance. The gaps between their description and their behavior are where the real insights live.

Reading the Interview

The best discovery interviews feel less like interviews and more like intrusions. You're asking someone to show you their messy, imperfect, workaround-filled reality — not to imagine a cleaner version of it for you. The sweet spot is somewhere between fascinated curiosity and mild discomfort. If the interview is going too smoothly, you're probably in gathering-opinions mode.

Pay attention to what people struggle to explain. Confusion in their own explanation usually means the problem is more complex than they thought, or they've never really examined it before. Either way, it's a signal.

Also pay attention to what they don't say. The gap between "this is annoying" and "I spent three hours on this last Tuesday" is where prioritization lives. Annoyance is universal; time and money are the currencies of priority.

The Post-Interview Test

After every discovery interview, ask yourself: did I learn something I didn't know, or did I just confirm what I already believed? Confirmation feels good. It also kills products. If every interview leaves you feeling validated rather than slightly unsettled, you're not doing discovery — you're doing theater.

The goal isn't to leave an interview with a feature to build. It's to leave with a better understanding of the problem — specific, behavioral, and grounded in what actually happened rather than what someone thinks might happen. Everything else is decoration.

title: The Metrics That Actually Guide Product Decisions
excerpt: Most product teams track too many metrics and understand too few. The problem isn't a lack of data — it's a lack of hierarchy. Here's how to build a metrics framework that tells you what to do next, not just how you did last week.
content:
The Dashboard Trap

A PM opens their morning dashboard: 47 metrics across 6 panels. Daily active users, retention by cohort, conversion funnel drop-off, average revenue per user, net promoter score, support ticket volume, feature adoption rates, session length, click-through rates on the new banner, and eighteen more. By 9:15am they've consumed all of it and still don't know what to work on today.

This is the dashboard trap: confusing visibility with direction. A metric that doesn't change what you do is decorative. A metric that changes what you do but points you in the wrong direction is dangerous. The entire point of product metrics is to compress a complex system into a signal you can act on — and most dashboards fail at both parts.

The Three-Layer Metric Hierarchy

Every product needs metrics at three levels, and confusing them is the most common cause of metric-driven paralysis:

1. The North Star: One Metric That Matters

This is the single number that, if it moved in the right direction, would mean your product is succeeding. Not "the most important metric" among many — the one metric that captures the core value your product delivers.

For a messaging app, it might be messages sent per active user per day — because if people aren't exchanging messages, nothing else matters. For a project management tool, it might be tasks completed per team per week — because completed tasks are the proof of value. For a marketplace, it's transactions facilitated, not GMV or listings, because a marketplace with high GMV and low transaction volume is just a very expensive listing site.

The north star is not always obvious. It's easy to pick a metric that's measurable rather than meaningful — "monthly active users" is the most common wrong answer because it's easy to track and almost never the actual thing you're trying to drive.

2. The Diagnostic Layer: Metrics That Explain the Why

When your north star moves, you need to know why. Diagnostic metrics are the 3-7 numbers that tell you what's driving changes in your north star. They are downstream and upstream of it — not unrelated KPIs you also happen to track.

If your north star is tasks completed per team per week, your diagnostic layer might include: tasks created per week (input), tasks marked complete per user (engagement depth), time from task creation to first action (activation speed), and weekly churn of teams (retention). If the north star drops, these tell you whether it's an input problem, an engagement problem, or a retention problem — each of which demands a different response.

The diagnostic layer should be small enough to hold in your head and connected enough that you can trace any north star movement to at least one diagnostic signal.

3. The Guardrail Layer: Metrics That Tell You What You're Breaking

Every product decision creates tradeoffs. Guardrail metrics watch the things you don't want to sacrifice — typically performance, reliability, trust, and user satisfaction. They don't tell you what to build; they tell you when you're building it too aggressively.

Common guardrails: page load time (don't ship features that make the product slow), error rate (don't ship features that break the product), support ticket volume per user (don't ship features that confuse people), and opt-out or unsubscribe rates (don't ship features that annoy people into leaving).

The critical property of a guardrail metric is that it should never be the thing you're optimizing for. If your north star is dormant for a quarter and your team starts optimizing the guardrail — say, driving support tickets to zero — you've lost the plot. Guardrails are constraints, not objectives.

How to Actually Use This Framework

The hierarchy only works if you use it differently at each layer:

  • North star: Review weekly. If it moved more than a meaningful threshold, trigger a diagnostic review. If it hasn't moved in a quarter, question whether it's the right north star.
  • Diagnostic: Review daily or weekly depending on velocity. These are the numbers you dig into when something changes. They should have owners — specific PMs or engineers who watch each one and can explain anomalies.
  • Guardrail: Set thresholds, not targets. "Page load under 2 seconds" is a constraint; "page load under 1.5 seconds" is an optimization target that pulls attention from real work. Alert when a guardrail breaches its threshold; don't report on it otherwise.

The Metrics Audit: A 30-Minute Exercise

If your current dashboard looks like most, here's what to do:

Step 1: List every metric you track. Everything on dashboards, in weekly reports, in Slack bots. Don't filter — just list them.

Step 2: For each metric, answer one question: "What decision would I make differently if this number changed by 20% tomorrow?" If you can't name a specific decision, the metric is decorative. Mark it.

Step 3: Assign every remaining metric to a layer. One north star. A handful of diagnostics connected to it. A few guardrails with thresholds. Everything else — even the useful-looking ones — goes into an "investigate later" pile.

Step 4: Delete or archive the decorative metrics. This is the hard part. Teams metastasize metrics the way they metastasize features — one stakeholder request at a time, never removed, always accumulating. A metric that hasn't changed a decision in six months is unlikely to start doing so. Remove it and see if anyone notices. If no one asks for it back in two weeks, it wasn't carrying its weight.

Step 5: Connect the remaining metrics. Draw the causal chain from diagnostics to north star. If you can't explain how a diagnostic metric influences the north star, it's probably measuring the wrong thing or measuring it wrong.

What This Gets You

A reasonable metrics framework doesn't tell you what to build — no metric does that. What it does is tell you, on a Tuesday morning, whether you should be worried, what specifically you should be worried about, and which numbers to ignore while you figure it out.

That's not nothing. Most PM time is spent deciding what to worry about. A good framework narrows that decision from "everything on the dashboard" to "the one number that matters and the three numbers that explain it."

The rest is noise. Learn to ignore it.
